preamble: A direct shift of the labiodental [f] to the alveolar sibilant [s] is very rare. The best-known case is word-initial fn- becoming sn- in Middle English, which turned earlier fnesen into snesen 'sneeze' and Old English fnora into snore. Because fn- was an unusual cluster, some scholars suggest the change began as a scribal misreading of fn- as ſn- (sn- with a long s), so its status as a purely phonetic change is debated. Romanian dialect forms such as Maramureș siérbe for fierbe 'boils' belong elsewhere: the sibilant that develops from f before front vowels there has a palatal timbre, distinct from primary [s].

examples.from: fnesen (Middle English), from Old English fnēosan
examples.note: Initial fn- became sn-; a competing explanation attributes the change to misreading fn- as ſn- (long s).
Same initial fn- > sn- change, which shows it was regular rather than a one-word accident.
